drafts.title: $0 and 3 seconds: look at the plug before you plug in (MAIN, today ~9 AM)
drafts.angle: A simple road-trip habit, tied to your own Kentucky drive. A damaged charger plug can bend a pin and take out the next car's charge port. Safety plus money, zero jargon.
bullets: IONNA pulled damaged CCS cables in Ohio, Indiana, Illinois and Missouri after reports a bad plug could bend a pin on the next car's port.
Fewer than two dozen cases out of more than 1 million IONNA sessions; Tesla-style (NACS) plugs not affected.
IONNA inspected 1,000+ connectors in four days and is running extra checks through the end of November.
Good advice on any network: if the pins look bent or the plug looks off, don't plug in. Move to the next stall.
drafts.body:
$0 and about 3 seconds. That's what it costs to look at a charger plug before you plug it in.

IONNA just pulled some bad CCS plugs in four Midwest states because a damaged one could bend a pin in the next car's charge port. They say it's rare, fewer than two dozen out of a million sessions. Still, a charge port repair is a dealer trip and a bill nobody wants on the road.

On my Kentucky drive I [stopped ___ times / plugged in at ___ stations] and honestly I [did / didn't] look at the plug first. I will now. If the pins look bent, I move to the next stall.

Tesla-plug owners are fine on this one. But it's a good habit for everybody, and a good one to pass along to anyone new to an EV.

Do you check the plug before you plug in?
drafts.ocr_why: Timely, practical, first-hand road-trip tie, easy yes/no reply, very saveable.
drafts.pixel: Hold a charger handle up to the camera: "Three seconds. Look at the pins. Here's why."
drafts.target: A verified EV news account posting the IONNA PSA (InsideEVs-style or @evwire), or IONNA's own account if active. Add your one-line road-trip take.

drafts.title: Colorado just made using your car as home backup a simple notice (Sun ~2 PM or Fri noon)
drafts.angle: Independence for families and older households. If the power goes out, your truck or EV can keep the essentials running, and Colorado just cut the red tape. Your personal stake: the one thing you can't lose in an outage.
bullets: Colorado PUC approved a settlement Oct 22, 2026 (Ford, Xcel, Black Hills).
Backup-only EV home power systems now need just a short notice (name, address, permit, "only when the grid is down"), not a utility approval process.
No penalty for skipping it, 60 days to fix, and anything installed before Oct 22 is exempt.
EVs that only charge need nothing. EVs that send power back while the grid is on still go through the full utility process.
Ford's system waits about 90 seconds after an outage and can't feed the grid.
drafts.body:
$0 and no permission slip. Colorado just made backing up your house with an EV a simple notice to the utility.

Before, it could turn into a back-and-forth with the power company. Now, if the car only powers the house when the grid is down, you send a short form and that's it. Already have one installed? You're grandfathered in.

At my house the thing I can't lose in an outage is [___ / my overnight medical equipment]. That's why I've been pricing home batteries, and a car that does double duty might be the cheaper middle step.

Would you use your car as backup power?
drafts.ocr_why: Colorado-local, new rule, personal stake. Keep "interconnection" and "settlement" out of your rewrite.
drafts.window: Sun ~2 PM MST or Fri noon-1 PM (not today, since your 6 AM post was already on power and batteries).
drafts.pixel: In the garage next to the car: "If the power goes out at 2 AM, here's what I'd want running."
drafts.target: A verified F-150 Lightning or Ford EV creator, or @SawyerMerritt if he posts home-backup news.

drafts.title: My road-trip posts could write a scam email to me (Tue ~9 PM or Sun ~8 PM)
drafts.angle: AI for the masses, scam edition. New study: everyday AI tools can turn your public posts into a personal scam email. Different from the Nov 2 paste-it-into-AI post; this one is "what you post is the bait." Lands hard for 55+ and their kids.
bullets: UT Arlington study (Nov 2): common AI tools pulled details from public posts and photos (trips, events, worries) to write personalized scam emails.
Default AI safety filters caught only 0% to 19% of those requests; with specific tuning, up to 99%.
SilverSafe: people 60+ reported about $3B lost to fraud in 2025; the typical reported loss for people 80+ was $2,000.
drafts.body:
$2,000. That's the typical scam loss for people over 80. And now AI can read your public posts and write the scam for you.

Researchers at UT Arlington had everyday AI tools look at public posts and photos, then write a personal scam email. Most of the tools didn't stop them.

I posted [my whole Kentucky trip ___, charging stops, prices] for anybody to see. A fake "charging receipt" or "toll notice" email that mentioned my real stops would've looked legit.

My one rule now, and the one I'm telling my family: if an email or text is about something you posted, don't click. Go to the site yourself.

Would you fall for one that knew your trip?
drafts.ocr_why: First-hand (your own public trip), fresh angle, gives one habit people share with parents.
drafts.window: Tue ~9 PM MST (top slot) or Sun ~8 PM.
drafts.pixel: Scroll your own trip posts on camera: "Everything a scammer needs is right here. Here's my one rule."
drafts.target: A verified fraud or consumer reporter, or an AI-for-seniors creator posting about AI scams.

drafts.title: +10%: Europe caps how fast FSD can go over the limit (Fri ~6 AM)
drafts.angle: Owner opinion. Europe put a speed cap on Tesla's self-driving. You drive I-70 with FSD; would you want that here? Easy reply bait for the Tesla crowd.
bullets: Dutch regulator RDW confirmed Tesla's update caps the speed margin at +10% over the limit (it was up to +50%), and it resets to 0 every time you start the car.
In Europe it's renamed "Tesla Assisted Driving" (was "FSD Supervised"), now recognized in 10 countries.
An EU-wide vote got pushed to December at the earliest.
drafts.body:
+10%. That's the most FSD can go over the speed limit in Europe now. And it resets to zero every time you start the car.

They also renamed it over there. It's "Tesla Assisted Driving" now, not FSD.

On I-70 I usually set mine to [___ over], mostly so I'm not the guy holding up traffic in the mountains. Having to reset it every single drive would drive me nuts.

Would you want a cap like that here, or leave it up to the driver?
drafts.ocr_why: Opinion hook drives replies; no dollar opener, so your own setting and the I-70 detail do the work.
